This overstays it's welcome. At first it felt like STALKER from the old days. Then it just kept dragging on. I've had several issues with reloading after dying. I'll hit load last save and then it will take me back to the death screen after a short loading screen. This has happened 10+ times in 20ish hours. Master difficulty is impossible, it wouldn't be if you could quicksave and plan better for the reload. Which was a core mechanic of these games before STALKER 2. Which was also dissapointing to me. STALKER was tough, but fair. It rewarded engaging with the mechanics and it never punished you for planning ahead. 
     This game doesn't allow you to plan ahead. You just get randomly ambushed by NPCs that spawned right behind you and you either die or waste 2/3 of your ammo and have to walk back to a trader so you can sell all the guns, buy more ammo and do it all over again. This is the reason I have 23 hours in this game. If that would stop happening I could just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ get on with it. Other STALKER games are fun, they don't overstay their welcome and they give you at least enough to get out of any situation. This gives you too much and then makes you waste most of it on ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 
     I play games for a challenge, but I also play to have fun. This is challenging, but it is not fun. It's beautiful. But the shooting mechanics are either headshots from stealth while NPCs have no clue you just shot their buddy with a non silenced rifle; or waste 2/3 of your health items and ammo trying to find that last guy shooting you from behind a tree from 600 yards away. Play if you want, it looks great. I'd personally rather play the old ones. They looked like ♥♥♥♥, but they were fun AF once you got used to how brutal they were. This is just brutal for the sake of being brutal and it doesn't even use the pain as a teacher. It just savages your poor little anus over and over again without any underlying lesson about tactics and planning. 
     Then you get better at firefighting and sticking to cover and you realize it actually isn't you like it was in the old STALKER games. The game is just like that. Which hurt my soul a little bit to be honest with you. I'd have rather had less story, potato graphics and a solid but brutal campaign. Instead I got a polished turd that seems to be making a commentary on modern abundance and how wasteful it has made all of us. Unless I missed something. I usually don't go in for moral lessons in games about shooting people in the face.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl — 3/10
I wanted this to be the Zone again. Fifteen years of waiting, a studio that actually lived through the thing the game is about, and a setting that still has no real competition. What shipped was a gorgeous, half-finished survival sim that keeps reminding you it isn’t finished.
The technical state is the review.

At launch this was not “Eurojank.” It was broken. Crashes, quest items that never spawn, NPCs vanishing mid-conversation, lighting that strobes, audio that dies, and death screens that make you wait long enough to question the purchase. Even after a year-plus of patches, an engine bump to Unreal 5.5, and a 2.0 overhaul, the game is still issuing 200-fix hotfixes in September 2026. That is not a living world. That is a product that never left the ICU.
Performance is still a tax. High settings on a strong rig should not feel like a coin flip. Settlements stutter. Open fields hitch. Textures pop in like the Zone is loading itself in front of you. If your machine is mid-range, you are not playing S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2. You are negotiating with it.
A-Life 2.0 is the betrayal.

This was the feature. The living Zone. Factions doing their own thing whether you were there or not. What we got was a spawn bubble. Enemies materialize behind you in ground you already cleared. Packs of dogs teleport into existence. Distant life barely exists until you walk into the radius, then the Zone “wakes up” like a scripted theme-park ride. Devs admitted they gutted it for optimization. Patches improved the worst of the air-spawns and back-spawns. They did not deliver the system that was sold. Binoculars and long-range play feel pointless when the world only exists 100 meters from your face.
AI on top of that is cheap more than clever. Mutants sponge damage, rush in waves, and punish you for playing carefully. Human NPCs flip between statue and aimbot. Stealth is inconsistent. Combat is loud, messy, and often decided by whether the engine decided to spawn three extra bloodsuckers in the doorway you just checked.
The systems fight you instead of the Zone.

Guns degrade and jam like they owe you money. Favorite rifles become junk mid-fight. Loot is stingy in the wrong places and weight management turns every outing into an inventory spreadsheet. Anomalies look great until you realize half the “danger” is just the game’s collision and detection being sloppy. Side content is a lot of walking for rewards that do not match the risk. Death-reload loops kill pacing. The Zone is huge; the interesting parts are not dense enough to justify how empty the travel feels when A-Life isn’t doing its job.
Story and presentation do not carry it.

The world looks like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Fog, decay, that sick green-gold light — when the frame rate holds, it is still one of the best atmospheres in the genre. Then someone talks. English VO is frequently stiff. Writing is functional at best and confused at worst. The main plot is a slog of fetch, faction errands, and twists that do not land. Branching paths exist on paper more than they change how the Zone feels. Side stories occasionally spark. The campaign as a whole does not.
What it should have been vs. what it is.

Ambition is not the problem. Scope is. They built a massive handmade map and then could not make the simulation, the AI, the performance, or the narrative keep up with it. The original games were janky and alive. This one is often just janky. Mods and later patches have done a lot of the work the launch build should have done. That is not a compliment. That is an admission.
If you have infinite patience, a high-end PC, and nostalgia strong enough to eat 40 hours of friction, there is still a tense, ugly, beautiful shooter under here. For everyone else: this is the sequel that asked you to wait a decade and a half and then charged full price for a beta that is still getting emergency patches in 2026.
The Zone deserved better. So did the people who waited.
Cheeki Breeki

you know, this game has had a bumpy road, ive heard all the hearsay and jargon, but i was experiencing a game drought, so as someone who quite enjoyed stalker gamma some 2 years ago, i decided to give it a try. i have never played the original trilogy, i wont pretend i have but i have done extensive research online about the trilogies lore and story back when i had a small stalker gamma phase. so i know what im talking about

THE GOOD:
- The story is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing, 4 endings, the original games actually matter, and everything makes sense in the end. 
- Gunplay feels very nice.
- plenty of choices, easter eggs and more that the world around you will react to
- the game is filled with nods to the original trilogy, and many familiar names will pop up if you played those.
- the open world is really ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cool.. and scary at times, i recommend not going underground if your a ♥♥♥♥♥ like me (unless the narrative forces you, which is more often than not)
- controls are easy to use, however i did remap my leaning keybinds because wtf is z and c for leaning left and right. 

THE BAD: 
- honestly the game can feel like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ walking simulator at times, and fast travel is hardly useful when you can only go to other settlements using it
- HUGE emphasis on walking simulator, its nice for taking the scenery in but it gets old fast (yes im mentioning this twice because holy it REALLY gets old fast)
- the gun customisation is kinda cheeks, but perhaps im just spoiled by escape from tarkov
- late game enemies are actual bullet sponges, i wont spoil, but youll see what i mean if you get that far

THE BOTTOM LINE:
honestly? i will strongly call this a 8/10 game, there is ABSOLUTELY room for improvement but all in all, especially considering the rumours i heard about this game, they arent true, at all. i have only had 2 crashes in the 39h i played and the game always ran smoothly, the games pacing is perfectly good and i genuinely had a blast clearing the story here. though i will say DO NOT buy this game if you are expecting a fleshed out survival game, grinding genuinely does not matter in this game, sure you can go do open world stuff and side quests, but it amounts to nothing in the end, at least for me.

DO buy this game if you want a good story over a binge of a few days, its been a long time, potentially years since i last played a game that had this good of a story, thats all from me, careful out there in the zone stalkers!

As I get older I've been gravitating more towards single player games. I haven't been able to find something I could really sink my time into for quite a few years now. Originally, I had bought the ultimate edition in 2024 when it first launched and played a little bit of it. I liked it but it didn't really grasp me. I would say since 2.0 came out with the DLC, I slowly started coming back to it and began to become obsessed with it. Fast forward to 9/5/2026. I took a week off of work and I put a little over 70 hours into my first playthrough before I got softlocked at the apartments while I was doing the DLC story yesterday. I uninstalled every mod, I quit and loaded the game, I looked online for a solution, nothing. Out of possible stubbornness I started a fresh playthrough, reinstalled all my mods and went back into the Zone with what I have learned. I'm almost 7 hours into the playthrough and have been enjoying every second of it from taking in the scenery to sitting in a room during an emission and playing the guitar for whoever is there with me, to being ambushed by bloodsuckers and boars to getting into firefights with bandits and finding artifacts. This is the first immersive sim I really played and sunk time into, minus System Shock 2 which has a third of what I put into it as I write this out and I never really had a game and its environment suck me in like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2 has. Even on my specs with FG, the world is stunning. The sounds are amazing and I love the music that I hear on the radio when I enter a bar for the first time. The tension I get from firefights is something I've never experienced in a game before and it has me coming back for more. To me, this is a game I could easily sink at least 1k hours into.

Give it a month after the zone kit is released to modders and you'll have Stalker Gamma 2.0 before you know it... base game is still phenomenal, but with modder support this game will change the standard for open world RPG post apocalyptic games.

It was a good S.T.A.L.K.E.R.

I enjoyed this game very much, it has its flaws but so did the originals , compared to the originals (without the hundreds of mods that have been made over the years) STALKER 2 is a big jump in quality especially in terms of story telling and character writing , sharing tragic stories of new and returning characters and asking some deep philosophical questions using the Zone as the main character.

Most of its flaws lie in the technical aspect, my main gripes were the NPC AI , A-Life with the infamous bubble , and how uninteresting the loot is (excluding the unique guns which I collected as many as I could). 

The AI could use a lot of work, first of all a bandit shouldn't behave the same as a trained soldier, but overall all of the AI needs to be more aggressive, use less aimbot, take better cover and react better but not in an unnatural way.

A-Life at the moment is kind of 'faking' a consistent world, you will come across skirmishes and small unscripted things while exploring but after a while it feels too samey and there really is not much depth to it at all, it just acts like a random AI spawner within 100 meters around you, and the 100 meters limit is very noticable, coming from G.A.M.M.A which has proper A-life implemented, the world in STALKER 2 feels surprisingly empty.

My last gripe with the game is the loot. Stashes feel very boring and unrewarding, in fact it's more exciting to search for them and the spots that the devs have hidden them than actually looting them and finding some ammo and sausages, with the exception of some unique guns and attatchments that I enjoyed collecting. There's also an abundance of ammo and grenades which doesn't feel very STALKER-y to me, especially in the early game.

However these 3 problems can be fixed in the future, and some are already massively improved by using mods which by the way the game has a bright future of modding ahead of it.

Now for the good stuff. 

Guns and gunplay feel amazing. The animations and sound are some of the best I have experienced in any FPS game, I enjoyed swapping attatchments in real time and having proper animations for it. The bossfights were each unique and memorable, because of different mechanics involved and the OST.

The sound is very immersive, there is a very noticable difference when being outside, in a building, a tunnel or a laboratory deep beneath the Zone. Also I appreciated the OST very much, it wasn't intruding when exploring in the open world or when having a minor fight with npcs, but it hit HARD when it needed to and added a lot to the bossfights, cutscenes and specific moments in the story.

Visuals after the 2.0 update are a bit too colourful but beautiful nevertheless, there is some artifacting when using DLSS but it got better with NVIDIA's 4.5 ray reconstruction update. There are some areas in the game that can make you believe that the Zone is a miracle after all, combined with the weather and the ambience this is one of the most atmospheric games I have ever played, and it makes you want to sit and enjoy the view in many cases.

The best part for me was the story and the characters, without spoiling anything, some of your choices really matter on the outcome and how the story plays out and evolves. In my opinion they did justice to all of the returning characters from the previous games and gave them a lot of depth that fits with the whole STALKER theme. Because the game is not linear and you might spend 10 hours exploring after going to the next main quest, the story might get a bit confusing, but there is a lot to uncover especially if you pay attention to detail and notes found in the world.

Overall would recommend, and with a few mods you can tailor the game more to the experience you want and get the most out of this game. Embrace the Zone.

Я бы не сказал, что стреляться здесь скучно, это скорее приятный тир, в котором иногда появляются ситуации, где нужно немного подзапариться. А так я больше умирал от гребанного "разбился на смерть" ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.  Ой как я люблю платформинг в этой игре, особенно в дополнении, когда тебе еще в глаза ссут. 

Сюжет прикольный, хоть и не вау. Дополнение тоже. Как обычно, в побочных квестах можно найти больше интересного. Но не смотря на богатый мир, работает он опять таки не на полную. Смысла в конфликтах фракций нет (чтобы потерять дружественный статус, надо просто в тупую расстрел устраивать; выбор стороны в квестах никак не влиял на общее отношение других фракций). Смысла в якобы симуляции дикой жизни мутантов тоже нет: если одни мутанты кусаются с другими мутантами, завидев вас, они все будут кусать только вас. Интересной экономики тоже нет, у всех торговцев плюс минус все одинаково, и где-то ближе к середине игры денег хватает на новую квартиру для Скифа. Да даже обычные нпс ощущаются все одинаково, за исключением нескольких из основной сюжетной.

Мелких багов тоже хватает. Например, вы не можете прострелить ветки и листья деревьев. А враги могут. Еще они могут стрелять с дробовика как со снайперской винтовки. В совокупности это дает незабываемые ощущения от перестрелок в лесу или в Припяти. Или вы можете застрять между двух бочек. 

Выбросы — раньше они и были круче, и смысла геймплейного в них было больше. А тут просто небо красное, которое пересидеть надо.

И как после всех этих компромиссов не ставится негативная оценка — черт его знает. В конечном итоге, я с удовольствием провел в этом мире много часов, прошел интересное приключение, проникся уникальной атмосферой и сильно так поностальгировал — не только по старому сталкеру и тому времени, но и в целом по какому-то олдовому ПК-геймингу.

STALKER 2 has been through a rough patch (not without good reason). Today, especially after update 2.0's sizable performance boost, STALKER 2 is a good STALKER game. Even a great one, that I would rank above Clear Sky at least. Does that mean it's going to be for everyone? No, and I don't think it needs to be. This game gets most of the important things right: a hauntingly beautiful open world to explore, satisfying tactical shooter-lite combat, addictive gear customization, and an intoxicating sense of mystery. The Chornobyl Exclusion Zone remains one of the most alluring and terrifying settings in all of gaming, full of deadly space-time anomalies and monsters to deal with as well as human bandits and mercenaries. It's a joy to explore and shoot your way through, with weighty gunplay and urban exploration that rewards caution and planning as well as quick reactions. I think newcomers migrating over from games like Metro Exodus will feel at home here, with some caveats. Enemies will still seem to spawn right next to you while wandering the Zone sometimes, which feels artificial and distracting. Scripted encounters at enemy bases and during missions always feel tense and tactical though, so I can forgive this. Headshots and accurate sharpshooting against human soldiers are just as important as in the original games, as are close-range shotgun blasts to keep charging mutants at bay. The combat is not very complex, but it feels excellent even after dozens of hours. There's a huge arsenal of weapons and armor suits to pore over and customize, with item descriptions that mostly do a good job of telling you what quality level they are. Upgrades are expensive though, and I can see some new players being frustrated with the economy or feeling like they upgraded the wrong thing. If you don't bring enough loot back to base after missions, it can be easy to run out of money, medkits, and ammo. I don't think STALKER would have the same appeal without some of these harsh mechanics though. There are no XP points or character levels - your own experience and knowledge of the Zone and how it works are what will lead you to success and better gear. That core philosophy is absolutely intact in STALKER 2, despite its rough edges.

If you have some idea of what you're getting into beforehand, I absolutely recommend STALKER 2. GSC Game World deserves their flowers for even getting this thing out the door while going through the hell that they did.

А сейчас, когда с геймплеем всё гораздо лучше, я могу спокойно посмотреть на историю. И если честно — ну а что я вообще ожидал? STALKER никогда не был игрой, которую я любил исключительно за сюжет. Это прежде всего атмосфера, исследование Зоны, звук, геймдизайн, оружие, артефакты, аномалии и ощущение того, что ты действительно находишься в этом мире.

На этом фоне сюжет STALKER 2 для меня сейчас выглядит вполне нормально. Он не какой-то невероятный шедевр, но он и не обязан им быть. На фоне всего остального он просто хороший элемент игры.

И, кстати, DLC это прекрасно показывает. Здесь сюжет мне реально нравится. Возможно, ещё и потому, что я наконец воспринимаю персонажей такими, какими их задумали разработчики, а не такими, какими я когда-то сам их себе придумал.

Когда я играл в старые части и читал диалоги, у меня в голове формировалось собственное представление о Стрелке, Шраме и других персонажах. На основе нескольких реплик, записок и событий я фактически сам достраивал их характеры. И если потом STALKER 2 показывал их иначе, естественно, возникало ощущение: «Что-то они не такие».

Хотя если посмотреть объективно, по материалам старых игр характер того же Стрелка можно было описать буквально в пару абзацев. Остальное мы сами дорисовывали у себя в голове.

А в DLC персонажи уже раскрываются гораздо непосредственнее, и поэтому их проще воспринимать именно такими, какие они есть в мире игры.

Но самое сильное впечатление от DLC у меня вообще не от сюжета.

Локации.

Там есть места, в которых я буквально останавливаюсь и начинаю всё рассматривать. Не потому что нужно искать какой-то тайник или предмет, а просто потому, что хочется посмотреть, как это всё сделано.

А «Пузырь» — это вообще что-то невероятное. Вот в такие моменты я понимаю, зачем мне был нужен STALKER 2.

Потому что именно тогда игра начинает ощущаться не как очередной сюжетный шутер с открытым миром, а как Зона, которую хочется исследовать просто из любопытства. Ты заходишь в какое-то место и не знаешь, что тебя там ждёт, а потом можешь минуту просто стоять и разглядывать окружение.

И вот сейчас я наконец могу сказать, что STALKER 2 стал той игрой, которую я когда-то представлял себе, играя в первую часть.

Не обязательно идеальной. Не обязательно с каким-то невероятным сюжетом. Но именно с тем ощущением Зоны, которое я когда-то дорисовывал у себя в голове.

Остаётся только A-Life.

И тут я прекрасно понимаю, почему с ним всё сложнее. Вернуть его в полноценном виде на уже существующую архитектуру игры, скорее всего, гораздо сложнее, чем просто «починить один баг». Возможно, когда-нибудь разработчики всё-таки смогут довести и эту систему до состояния, которого все ждут.

И если это произойдёт, то лично для меня STALKER 2 окончательно станет тем самым STALKER, которого я ждал ещё с первой игры.

We have a huge responsibility to GSC Game World, who gave us treasured moments and adventures in our previous travels into the Zone!

My fellow stalkers, I have been far from the Zone up until the time of writing about my experiences.
There are new factions, a much bigger world, references and returning locations and characters from [i]Shadow of Chernobyl[/i], [i]Clear Sky[/i], and [i]Call of Pripyat[/i]. For us older stalkers, seeing returning characters who can now actually speak, since we are no longer playing a mute protagonist, was a really nice addition. I grew attached to quite a few of them.

New mutants that were once only ideas that never made it into the previous games have finally made their way into [i]S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2[/i], along with plenty of new guns, upgrades, suits, and artifacts. The returning mutants have also been buffed. Yes, I say this with a somewhat annoyed expression on my face.

Got 400 rounds for your current gun? Easily spent on some of the tougher varieties of mutants. They can be absolute bullet sponges. At least, you can occasionally get trophies from them that can be sold or used in side missions for some extra money.

The different endings allow for multiple playthroughs, but I will say this: buying new gear, repairs, and upgrades is [b]VERY[/b] expensive. Be prepared to grind, budget your money, and plan carefully around the equipment you already have.

Overall, [i]S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2[/i] feels like a worthy return to the Zone. It has plenty of familiar elements for veterans while introducing enough new content to make the journey feel like more than a simple nostalgia trip.

I've put about 30 hours into this game, and am really disappointed that I have to not recommend. I will say, it's a negative review with something of an asterisk, however. This game may still be for you, but if you are a fan of the original trilogies, Anomaly, or the rare breed who loved both equally, this game will fail on almost all points to impress. Stalker 2 is a confused game, and that leads to perculiarities.

I will begin by giving credit where it is due, from what I can tell, 2.0 appears to have fixed a great many performance issues. Naturally, audio/visual is excellent. The Zone looks how you remember, but better. There has clearly been inspiration taken from the modding community of the original games for stuff like animations, availability of guns, modification therein, and smaller, immersive things. All of this is generally good stuff, I've applauded it, none of it has overstayed its welcome in the 30 hours I took a run at this game. 

The story, and player character are also good stuff. No complaints. The quality here may have even improved, which is what you can and should ask for in a sequel. Skif is a particularly enjoyable character, and the returning faces have managed to be more than nostalgia-bait. Former player characters have changed enough that newcomers to the series will have no trouble getting to grips with their new factions and motivations,  but series veterans will not feel alienated. I suspect, like me, you will want to power through the story with few distractions.

The actual act of artifact hunting, too, has been improved in my view. It's much more entertaining, about as challenging as in the past, and you get the little dopamine hit of being able to look at whatever you pull out of the anomaly field. Some can be exceptionally tricky to get safely, particularly in gravity anomalies. 

If only any of it had a point. Even the perks of attaching an anomaly, beyond ones that buff your damage resistance, is questionable. 

This is the crux of my issues with the game, it's not good enough on its own merits to be a shooter, and not immersive enough to be an immersive survival sim. It has tried to thread the needle between the two  broad communities of players it seeks to attract, and has not succeeded on either point. I have three issues in particular.

1. The AI: It's ♥♥♥♥♥, even with the Herculean efforts of modders. At its best, they'll pose a danger in the mid-to-late game due to their better equipment, and the fact they are immersively-breakingly cracked out. The problem is, cracked-out as they may be (you will take accurate fire for the briefest exposure), they are also ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brain dead. Even if you get a Mod, as I did, that has them take cover, and approximate suppresing fire, it will likely fail to break their ESP, and they are still susceptible to cheese. Draw some aggro, camp a corner. Alternatively, blow them away at extended range and watch the AI fail to come up with a good solution for this. It's not particularly fun, and it's certainly not challenging, and I am hard pressed to point out a single example of an actual 'firefight.' 

This is, ostensibly, a shooter with survival elements. You need to generally be careful, in theory, because the ability to sustain a fight (meds, ammo), is scarce. The latter is true only if you're looting, but at the standard difficulties you will never be broke, and will routinely walk around with ammo akin to someone going on a jungle hump in Vietnam. Meds are a plenty, and will you need them, and you will routinely, without second thought, churn through 10-15 medkits in a fight as both you and the AI sponge up punishment you mete out to each other. Worry not, though, because every other body will have healing items on them, and every location will have boxes upon boxes to crack open with your knife. Which leads me to my second point...

2. There's no scarcity at any of the standard difficulties. This is a direct result of (1), clearly. You will never have to go out of your way to get gear and kit for the next challenge. You will, often, have it fall directly into your laps (a notorious example is during the underground segment at the SIRCAA facility). I played the game largely linearly and found myself drowning in currency, meds, food, supply, etc. Never did I have to stop the march onwards, or deviate, to do some sidequests for cash, or stash coordinates, etc. This is absolutely a break, in my view, with the core vision of the game world you're supposed to be in. It may not be a deal breaker for you, so an asterisk on my negative review is appended here, but it's absolutely a no-no for me. Which leads me to my final gripe...

3. There's little reason to immerse yourself. The zombie-corpse of GSC broke out of their coffin to render the Zone, lovingly, in the latest Unreal engine, and there's hardly incentive, or reason, to see much of it. Now, here you may accuse me of not going out of my way to do so, but the issue is not only do I not need to, the lack of need is making me not want to. More pressingly, you often find yourself compelled to keep going, and particularly after the attack on SIRCAA you will find yourself running something of a gauntlet, from one set-piece to the next. 

The original games, and their mods, did a very good job of creating a loop where side activities did a good job of disguising themselves as vitally important to advancing the plot of the main game. They provided you with the resources to keep going North, to the heart of the Zone, and essentially provided you with anti-frustration equipment married with additional gameplay content. You will never, and I do mean never, feel compelled to do that in Stalker 2. You can go essentially from the opening set piece in the Burned Forest, right to Zalissya, and thereafter through to the end game with very few reasons to stop if you are somewhat mercenary with your equipment and armour. If you have pet guns and kit, you may occasionally find yourself breaking the pace to repair and replenish their ammo, but will hardly need to go out of your way to get the resources to do so, you'll not have a shortage of them. Nor will you want to, as I touched upon, because the actual gameplay is rather bland when you get into trouble.

The addition of a custom difficulty, which does require a new game, and a burgeoning modding community, may finally address these issues for good. I will only caution you to remember this: It took a decade for the original games' modding community to get their creations to release candidacy quality, and Stalker 2 was in development for almost that long. You can, no, should, demand way more of a dev charging you 80 CAD or 50 Quid for a product in such a confused (and I do mean confused in every sense of the word) state.

I could write an essay about everything that I liked and disliked about S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2, but to keep it short: I do recommend it.

The atmosphere alone makes it worth it. Not once did I get tired of exploring the zone. It is so much fun to go around and recognize all the places from the old games. The weather effects also bring it to another level.
The gameplay is good overall, thanks to solid gunplay and the fact that GSC managed to avoid the tedium of many open world games that end up being giant collectathon. Here, exploration is the main drive and I really liked it.

Optimization, which is often a giant pain point with Unreal Engine 5, was extremely solid. High settings, 1440p native and the game ran around 80 to 100 fps for the vast majority of the time while going around the zone. There was an occasional hitch when the game would autosave or when the infamous "traversal stutters" kicked in, but that was a really smooth ride otherwise. Absolutely 0 crash to report as well.

I'm quickly going to complain about the lack of depth of the health system, with poor Skif turning into a mummy full of needle holes, the abundance of loot that ends up robbing the game of any sense of difficulty, or the fact that A-Life feels like things are happening in a 100m bubble around the player. But. Given the context in which the game was made and how ambitious of a project it is, I can't really be mad at it. Except that very last room at the end of the game. Screw that. If you know, you know.

Even with these shortcoming, this was a really good time and the 60-something hours I've spent on beating the base game flew by.

Fallout: Chornobyl is probably the best game in the entire Fallout franchise. By far. Somehow this supposed Slav Jank has about a twentieth of the jank of actual FO games, several hundred percent more immersion, an absolutely magnificent story and setting, and a world I can lose myself in for hours on end. 

Probably the biggest key word there is immersion. The genius of not having an RPG leveling/stat system is probably the best possible thing you can do to achieve that. When you don't have that XP bar taunting you, you suddenly start weighing entirely different priorities like... not dying. Seeing a spooky place that gives you a bad vibe? Yeah maybe saving your resources and your cheeky britches feels like the smarter option. A chaotic gunfight kicks off between friendlies and bad guys? Better have some trigger discipline because they're going to be tricky to tell apart. Got a really nice gun and armor? Hope you can afford to pay for the repairs and exotic ammo. You wheezing under the weight of loot and found another stash? Tough luck, you're not fast traveling to a store and back. Combine this with absolutely gorgeous, beautiful visuals and lighting and you have the most immersive experience available on PC right now.

I have never felt more desperate. I have never felt more frightened. I have never felt more alive. 

... in a game at any rate, but you quickly forget that you're playing one.

It's a broken game with fragmented storyline - trying to do a lot of things altogether and failing at all of them in more miserable ways than one.

I purchased AFTER the 2.0 update and never played STALKER 1 - so I was giving it a fair chance. Just finished it because of the sake of being a gamer and my hard earned money already invested in it - glad I did not go for the DLC's or Ultimate Edition. I will never play any series of this game again. One and Done!

Beyond the crashes that occur far too frequently, the bullet-sponge NPCs, the mission trigger glitches, and terrible physics - the fundamental problems are too many to ignore:

1 - Game is trying to bring together already established and popular genres and game mechanics into a single IP which is downright impossible and also not ideal - METRO, Call of Duty, Last of Us and many more - while it fails at all of them.

2 - Everyone in the zone is a typical ideological lunatic - which no thread of pragmatism that the player can associate with. All choices are forced and not really organic - you get to choose between worse and much worse - which adds to the frustration of an already broken game to the point that you just want to be over with it.

3 - Characters are neither likeable nor relatable - and Skif just gets reduced to an errand boy for everyone fetching pieces from one corner of the map to another, with no agency of his own - making this game a walking simulator for the most part. Press W - move the mouse around - repeat (for hours)

4 - Regardless of how much you upgrade, gear-up, level-up, finish missions, save people, save bases - there is never really any autonomy rewarded to the player to be able to feel like we are earning a reputation while saving the zone one mission at a time - it just goes back to being a runner for people.

The ENDINGS - are all just as worse as the gameplay design itself - no real closures, no real satisfaction of achieving something or making a substantial change in the lives of people or the zone itself. Just back to square one - hands change - the zone is still the zone. So Skif wasting 100+ hours in it does absolutely nothing.

I waited until 2.0 was released and here is what I think..

The world are immersive and felt good at first, perhaps at the first 0-15 hours but after that they felt quite tedious and I'm just at garbage region. 

- A lot of walking/running involved that reminds me of Death Stranding vibes (this one uses bike though). 
- The mutants are very spongy and it got worse when coupled with anomalies
- Many of the anomalies you have to find out how they behaves yourself, which means get damaged and killed many times
- Majority of the artifacts so far does not seems useful or interesting, they felt useless due to its + and - stats
- The detention center basement (garbage region) psychic mutant + fire anomalies is a very questionable level design. Not only that, the artifact in that area is also doesn't make sense. I got burned like at least 50 times. I've beaten dark souls 1 2 3, elden ring, sekiro but this...this is a whole new masochist design.
- A lot of fetch/empty quests that are not memorable (storyline + rewards wise), does not make much sense but you just want to complete it for the sake of completing another x side quest
- There are many unexplained things which requires you to research online
- Somehow the only obvious way to know whether you can attack the person is whether thew white detection meter start filling up or not, and this is probably the most common experience most people had I am sure
- All types of human enemy can instantly see you most of the time if you're not careful, leading to reloading saved game usually. They seem to be highly accurate as well (like above average shooter)
- I saw people mention that you have to know a lot of the details in the past stalker's game (which means usually played them), otherwise Stalker 2 wont make much sense, that is quite unfortunate in terms of storytelling for people who forgot them or newcomers to the franchise.

There are good things and more negative points I am sure but this is just my experience so far up to garbage region. I can say Stalker 2 isn't a bad game but they are overall mediocre and not able to hold my attention for any longer than 25-35 hours.

I played this game for a little over an hour and it is genuinely worse in every aspect compared to previous STALKER games.  
First off, you can't loot mutants.  WTF.  There is ZERO point to engaging mutants then, which means that a large part of the enemies in the game you are better off just avoiding.   Looting mutants has been super fun in previous games, especially for the rarer mutants like controllers and pseudogiants.  
Second, I guess this is UE5 but the movement is super clunky and not enjoyable.  The games based on the X-ray engine felt hyper responsive and performant.  The performance of STALKER 2 is abysmal I have a 9950X and a 5090 and I can't run the game consistently above 90FPS at 4k WITH reduced settings.  
Third, the gunplay is ass.  Everything is a bullet sponge(blasted poltergeist took like 4 AK rounds to kill) and bandits with no armor body 3-4 shots to the chest from an AR for whatever reason.   
Fourth, they add animations to everything which slows the game down immensely.  In the first mission you have to put this beacon thing down and it uses up like 5-6 seconds to deploy it each time which totally takes you out of the game.  In the previous games you would press F and it would simply appear on the ground which is honestly better because you stay in control the whole time.  
I'm sure if I kept playing I'd find dozens more things that sucked or were a huge downgrade from previous games, but I already had enough disappointment in the little time I spent playing the game. 

If you want to enjoy STALKER, for the love of all that is fun just download Anomaly.  Or if you want way more immersion and features download Gamma I guess, I hear its good.  

Do not buy this game.  It is not even a good game in its own right, let alone a good STALKER game.  I read that the people who developed this game did not work on the original games, which makes perfect sense.

-Mutants lacked the same level of depth as the ones in Metro and Fallout. Metro's mutants have engaging mechanics. Fallout's had limb damage/destruction. review.review:
The developers’ incredible efforts to improve the game with every update (which come out very frequently) are simply mind-blowing. I have endless respect for them for not abandoning it like 90% of game studios do; you could say they’ve poured their hearts into this game and continue to do so.

The game itself features beautiful graphics, a story with many branching paths, and that very same atmosphere that made us fall in love with it in the first place.

Stalker 2: Heart of Chornobyl — A Hilarious Review for a Game That Wants You Dead (Lovingly)
Stalker 2 is the only game where you can step outside, take a deep breath, admire the hauntingly beautiful sky… and immediately get vaporized by an anomaly that sounds like a microwave having a panic attack. It’s a masterpiece of terror, jank, brilliance, and pure Slavic chaos wrapped in one radioactive burrito.

The Zone: A Place Where Hope Goes to Die
The Zone in Stalker 2 is gorgeous—like “I want to take a screenshot and frame it” gorgeous. But don’t get too comfortable. Every time you stop to admire the scenery, something behind you is already plotting your funeral.
Mutants? Everywhere.
Bandits? Always behind you.
Anomalies? Invisible landmines with personality disorders.

It’s the only game where gravity itself occasionally decides it’s done with your nonsense.

Gunfights That Feel Like Job Interviews
Combat in Stalker 2 is incredible… when it works. Guns feel weighty, realistic, and satisfying. But sometimes they jam, misfire, or simply refuse to acknowledge your existence. It’s immersive, sure, but also feels like your AK is judging your life choices.

You’ll line up the perfect shot, breathe in, squeeze the trigger…
click  
Your gun: “No.”
The mutant: “Dinner.”

Inventory Management: The True Final Boss
You will spend 40% of your playtime looting, 40% organizing your loot, and the remaining 20% crying because you’re overweight by 0.3 kilograms and must decide whether to drop ammo or the 17 cans of tuna you panic-looted earlier.

NPCs With the Emotional Range of a Brick
Every NPC looks like they’ve seen things that would break a therapist. They speak in riddles, threats, or the kind of philosophical one-liners that make you question your own existence.

You ask for directions.
They tell you about the nature of suffering.
You still don’t know where the objective is.

A Game That Hates You… But You’ll Love It Anyway
Stalker 2 is terrifying, punishing, glitchy, atmospheric, and absolutely unforgettable. It’s the kind of game where you rage-quit, uninstall, reinstall, and then spend six more hours wandering the Zone because you need to know what’s behind that creepy abandoned factory.

It’s terrible.
It’s amazing.
It’s Stalker 2.

Final Verdict
Stalker 2 is the best worst time you’ll ever have.  
If you enjoy atmospheric survival, brutal gunfights, and being bullied by physics itself, welcome to the Zone.
If not… well, the Zone will welcome you anyway. It always does.

It took me a bit to get into the game. The recent update helped and the graphics have definitely improved. Once the game clicks and draws you in, it's genuinely pretty fun. You realize the zone is a dangerous place and roaming around between areas feels like an adventure where you're not sure what you'll encounter. You rely on scavenging ammo, weapons, and supplies, which forces you to explore the abandoned buildings. This is mostly fine, but it does get a bit old after awhile and you'll eventually be overloaded with common items like bread, bandages, and sausage. You need to keep an eye on the amount of weight you're lugging around because too much can slow you down. I found myself mostly encumbered just carrying the basics of food, ammo, two weapons, and armor. Ammo is readily available, but given all the different types, you'll find it hard to have the right kind of ammo for the gun you want to carry if you rely on scavenging alone. It's best to just buy lots of your preferred type at the next trading post. Buying ammo and paying to repair your gear is very expensive and will drain most of your credits. Make sure to carry back some spare loot to sell to offset the cost.

The zone feels vast and eerie and there are some terrifying moments. It takes a bit of practice to figure out how to deal with the mutants and how to pick the best weapon loadout to deal with the majority of enemies. I found myself using the VS Vintar for humans to silently snipe them at mid-range and a shotgun (sawed off and eventually a cracker) to deal with mutants. Fighting some of the harder mutants can feel a bit silly as they'll kill you quickly if you face them head on. It often requires using some gimmicky tactics to beat them, like retreating into a building that the mutant can't fit in or spamming them with grenades. Initially, most encounters felt very difficult until I learned to use head shots to quickly end most fights with other human-like enemies. 

There is a lot of content in this game, and it's easy to get sidetracked with side missions. As I don't have all the time in the world, I just focused on the main mission as it also is very engaging and takes long enough to beat on its own. From what I can see though, I could easily spend another 400 hours roaming around the Zone doing side missions and collecting loot. I find it funny that there are so many reviews for this game 100-200+ hours of gameplay giving a "Not Recommended" rating. Clearly there is something to this game if you're spending that much time playing it. For my part, I intend to move along after I wrap up the main story. I may try the DLC, but I don't enjoy playing filler content or trying to do "completionist" tasks like collecting all special items (ex. artifacts) or trying to scavenge all the special stashes. The game requires a lot of running between areas. This is initially a pretty fun way to explore, but over time it becomes tiresome when you're trying to do side missions or collect artifacts.

Anyway, give the game a try and know that you'll need to stick with it for 10-15 hours before it starts to click. There is more than enough content to justify the price, but it depends how much you enjoy side missions, hunting down special items, and scavenging as to whether you'd want to try to see all of it. The main mission alone fills enough space though and with branching pathes offers some replayability, so you can go back and make different choices.

**An incredible survival experience!**

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. 2: Heart of Chornobyl is an amazing game for fans of atmospheric open-world shooters. The Zone feels mysterious, dangerous, and incredibly immersive, with a dark atmosphere that keeps you exploring and wondering what you will find next.

The gunplay is satisfying, the environments look beautiful, and the survival elements add a lot of tension. Exploring abandoned buildings, searching for supplies, and dealing with dangerous mutants and other enemies makes every journey feel unpredictable.

The story and atmosphere are definitely the highlights, making the game feel like a true adventure through the Zone.

**Highly recommended for fans of survival, horror, and FPS games!**

There are some valid criticisms, like some of the mechanics not being particularly deep but what this game has in abundance is atmosphere. It has all of the atmosphere. It drips with atmosphere.

Stalker is a pleasure just to walk around in, in the same way that a lot of people play RDR2 just to ride their horse around.

The map is big and detailed, graphics are decent.

But the gameplay is incredibly shallow and generally frustrating, the itemization simply isn't complex enough to warrant the amount of time sunk killing the same NPCs over and over and over (and getting the exact same weapons, over and over and over). As an example, I used the same rifle for almost 20 hours of gameplay straight because there simply wasn't a good reason to use anything else once I found it. The artifacts that are supposedly valuable and have unique effects are just stat buffs with no unique effects at all, and most of them have such a small effect that they are pretty much pointless.

The survival-ish systems are super basic and feel like they are entirely tacked on, at no point ever was I struggling to keep good food or resource stores and boiled down to reflexively eating and sleeping whenever the icons told me to do so, there is zero functional difference between all foodstuffs other than better ones fill you up faster (they provide no benefit outside of that).

There are many questionable design elements at play that seem to be there just to make the game more frustrating for the player, not in a "this is difficult but rewarding to manage" way, in a "this feels entirely designed around just making things arbitrarily more tedious for no reason".

There are still very large bugs present in the game, I have lost over 3 hours to backtracking due to them.

I have steadily added more and more mods to remove or change multiple things about the game to make it more palatable and less grating.

I want to like it, and I want to recommend it, but I can't there just isn't much here other than the gigantic open map that is noteworthy.
